Use of nanobubble water bioaugmented anaerobically digested sludge for
high-efﬁcacy energy production from high-solids anaerobic digestion of
corn straw
Xuezhi Wang a,c, Zhongfang Lei b,⁎, Zhenya Zhang b, Kazuya Shimizu b,d, Duu-Jong Lee e, Samir Kumar Khanal f

H I G H L I G H T S
G R A P H I C A L
A B S T R A C T
• NBW enhanced enzymatic activities and
microbial community during bioaugmen-
tation.
• NBW augmented sludge enhanced ligno-
cellulose degradation in high-solids AD.
• 47% higher CH4 yield was detected in O2-
NBW augmented sludge high-solids AD.
• No increase in reactor volume is realized
in NBW augmented sludge high-solids AD.
A B S T R A C T
A R T I C L E
I N F O
Editor: Qilin Wang
Keywords:
Nanobubble water
High-solids anaerobic digestion
Agricultural waste
Renewable energy recovery
Bioaugmentation
An increasing attention has been paid to the secure and sustainable management of agricultural wastes, especially lig-
nocellulosic biomass. Nanobubble water (NBW) contains 106–108 bubbles/mL with diameter <1000 nm. Although
previous studies have examined the enhancement effects of NBW on methane production from organic solid wastes,
the NBW-based anaerobic digestion (AD) system is still restrained from practical application due to the large increase
in AD reactor volume, generation of wastewater, and increase in energy consumption as well. In this study, NBW bio-
augmentation of anaerobically digested sludge for the ﬁrst time was performed for high-solids AD of corn straw. Re-
sults show that cellulase, xylanases and lignin peroxidase activities were increased by 2–55% during the NBW
bioaugmentation process. Signiﬁcant enrichment of hydrolytic/acidogenic bacteria and methanogenic archaea were
noticed in the NBW bioaugmented sludge. This study clearly demonstrated 47% increase in methane production
from high-solids AD of corn straw when O2-NBW bioaugmented sludge was applied, achieving a net energy gain of
5138 MJ/t-volatile solids of corn straw with an energy recovery of 34%. The NBW-based high-solids AD system can
provide a novel and sustainable management solution for renewable energy production from agricultural wastes,
targeting the reduction of environmental pollution and energy crisis.

1. Introduction
With the emergence of COVID-19 and post-COVID manufacturing in-
dustries, environmental pollution and energy crisis have become one of
the most important socio-economic issues (Carbon Brief Ltd, 2021). The
currently over reliance on fossil fuels has led to concerns on climate change
and energy security. Therefore, new policies are urgently needed to reduce
greenhouse gases (GHGs) emission, increase the recycling of waste bioma-
terials, and accelerate the development of circular economy. Anaerobic di-
gestion (AD) has been widely applied for agricultural residues and organic
wastes for decades to produce biogas that can further be used for electricity
generation or thermal energy, thus reducing GHGs emission and fossil fuels’
consumption.
Agricultural waste (mainly lignocellulosic biomass) is a promising and
sustainable feedstock for the production of fuels, chemicals and other valu-
able products due to its abundance worldwide and enormous availability
(Croce et al., 2016). However, the primary barrier hindering its widespread
application is the low energy recovery from raw feedstocks via AD. Various
pretreatments have been attempted to enhance the hydrolysis step, includ-
ing physical (grinding, irradiation, and ultrasonic) (Zheng et al., 2014),
chemical (acid and alkali) (Li et al., 2020), and biological (enzymatic, fun-
gal) (Muaaz-Us-Salam et al., 2020) methods. However, in terms of energy
balance, these pretreatment methods to a great extent make the whole sys-
tem difﬁcult to be compensated by the increased CH4 yield. In addition,
they also generate toxic by-products that are neither economical nor sus-
tainable.
Development of sustainable energy production schemes is one of the
most important scientiﬁc challenging subjects in the 21st century (Liu
et al., 2010). As reported, nanobubble water (NBW) exhibits great poten-
tials for the enhancement of bioenergy generation (Wang et al., 2021).
NBW contains 106–108 bubbles/mL with diameter <1000 nm (Lyu et al.,
2019). These nanobubbles (NBs) possess the following features including
high speciﬁc surface area, hydrophobic property, high mass transfer rate,
longevity, high mobility and diffusion of water molecules, capability to gen-
erate free radicals, etc. (Movahed and Sarmah, 2021). Therefore, NBs have
been widely applied in various ﬁelds, including marine environments,
water disinfection, membrane defouling, etc. (Lyu et al., 2019). Nowadays,
much attention has been paid to the application of NBW in agricultural
waste (lignocellulosic biomass) management due to its high mobility and
diffusion of water molecules, zero pollution, and relatively low energy con-
sumption. One of the most amazing properties is its improvement effect on
the physiological activity of living organisms (Ebina et al., 2013). NBW has
been proven to enhance methane production from waste activated sludge
via AD (Wang et al., 2019). Yang et al. (2019) found that addition of
NBW enhanced hydrolase activities in AD of waste activated sludge. NBW
can also greatly enhance the hydrolysis-acidiﬁcation stages of high loading
AD systems (Wang et al., 2020b). Hou et al. (2021) reported that NBW can
improve the coenzyme F420 activity at the methanogenesis stage in the two-
stage AD of food waste. Most recently, O2-NBW supplementation was
proven capable of creating a more favorable microaerobic environment
for facultative microbes to degrade organic solid waste via AD process
(Wang et al., 2021; Hou et al., 2021), which has been successfully applied
in wet AD systems for enhanced methane production from lignocellulosic
biomass by 20–30% when compared to the control (Wang et al., 2020c).
Nevertheless, the large volume increases in AD reactor and wastewater (liq-
uid digestate) generation due to the direct addition of NBW lead to high op-
eration costs and energy consumption, limiting the practical application of
NBW in AD systems.
Bioaugmentation technology has been attempted to recover energy
from ammonia-rich substrates to alleviate ammonia toxicity, achieving
31% increase in methane yield due to 5-fold increase in relative abundance
of Methanoculleus sp. (Fotidis et al., 2014). Martin-Ryals et al. (2015)
claimed that the continuous bioaugmentation of cellulolytic microbial con-
sortia can improve the methanogenic performance. As reported, the meth-
ane yield can be increased by 10–22% from wet AD of corn straw when
NBW pre-augmented anaerobically digested sludge was used (Wang et al.,
2020a). However, the slightly increased CH4 yield by the NBW-based wet
AD technology to a great extent makes it difﬁcult to compensate for the in-
creases in energy consumption and biogas slurry production volume by the
system due to NBW addition. In addition, the related mechanism of NBW
bioaugmentation is still unclear, especially from the enzymatic and micro-
bial levels in the pre-augmentation process.
High-solids AD (with total solids (TS) content ≥10%) is a promising al-
ternative for organic solid waste management due to its high volumetric
productivity, less heating energy consumption, much less or little liquid
digestate production, and higher methane yields than wet AD. Up to the
present, little information is available regarding the energy balance analysis
of NBW-based AD systems, especially under high-solids conditions.
Therefore, in addition to the underlying mechanisms, this study aimed
to ﬁgure out the effects of NBW-bioaugmented sludge on lignocellulosic
degradation and methane production potential of corn straw under high-
solids AD condition. The impact of NBW-bioaugmented sludge was ﬁrstly
analyzed with respect to microbial communities and enzymatic activities.
Then, the renewable energy production from high-solids AD of corn straw
was evaluated in terms of methane yield. Finally, the major advantages of
NBW-based high-solids AD technology were clariﬁed based on energy
gain analysis. The novel NBW-based high-solids AD system is expected to
be more conducive to practical applications for energy production from lig-
nocellulosic biomass, serving the sustainable society.
2. Materials and methods
2.1. Raw materials and anaerobically digested sludge
The ensiled corn straw was sampled from a local farm operated by
Japan Agricultural Co-operatives in Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. The corn
straw was dried at 60 ± 1 °C to a constant weight and ground to pass
through a 0.6 mm sieve, and then stored at room temperature before exper-
iments. Anaerobically digested sludge was collected from the Shimodate
Wastewater Treatment Plant in Chikusei, Ibaraki Prefecture, Japan. Before
being used, the sludge was ﬁltered through a 1-mm sieve and digested at 35
± 1 °C for 7 days to activate microbial activity and decompose the remain-
ing easily biodegradable organics. The main characteristics of corn straw
and anaerobically digested sludge were described elsewhere (Wang et al.,
2020a). The NBW used in this research was produced by a NBW generator
(HACK, FB11, Japan). N2 and O2 (with a purity of 99.9995%) gases used for
NBW generation were purchased from Taiyo Nippon Sanso Co., Ltd.
(Japan). 1 L deionized water (DW) in a 5 L plastic beaker was injected
into the NBW generator. During the NBW generation, the pressure was con-
trolled at 0.22–0.25 MPa (25 ± 1 °C). The gas intake speed and DW circu-
lation ﬂow rate were controlled at 0.05 L/min and 3 L/min, respectively.
After 20 min generation, the number of bubble particles was around 3 ×
108 particles/mL with the particle size <200 nm. These data were similar
with the characteristics of NBs obtained by Hou et al. (2022) and Wang
et al. (2019).
2.2. Bioaugmentation of anaerobically digested sludge by deionized water, N2-
NBW, and O2-NBW
In order to avoid the production of large amount of liquid digestate and
increase in reactor volume caused by the direct NBW addition, use of NBW
to augment the digested sludge ﬁrst to enhance microbial community and
enzymatic activity is regarded as a promising solution for efﬁcient energy
recovery from AD of corn straw. The bioaugmentation of anaerobically
digested sludge was performed in 600 mL serum bottles under the addition
of deionized water (DW), N2-NBW or O2-NBW. Each bottle with a working
volume of 400 mL was added with 200 mL of anaerobically digested sludge
and 200 mL of NBW or DW. Corn straw as the only substrate was added into
the bottle with no addition of other substances like macro- and/or micro-
nutrients.
Addition of
corn straw was controlled at
a food-to-
microorganisms (F/M, volatile solid (VS) basis) ratio of 1.5 at the beginning
of each pre-augmentation. After being well mixed, the pH was adjusted to

7.00 ± 0.05 with 2.0 M NaOH or HCl. Then, the AD reactors were sub-
jected to 5 min of N2 ﬂushing to create anaerobic conditions. All the pre-
augmentation tests were performed in a thermostatic container at 35 ± 1
°C. The digestion residue was centrifuged at 5000 rpm for 10 min to remove
the supernatant when methane production was <1% of the accumulated
volume of methane during three consecutive days (Holliger et al., 2016).
2 mL of the digested sludge was sampled from each bioreactor during
each bioaugmentation cycle (about 30 days) for the determinations of cel-
lulase (CMCase), xylanase, and lignin peroxidase (LiP) activities. After the
designated bioaugmentation cycles, the efﬂuent from the AD reactor with
DW or NBW addition was concentrated by centrifugation at 6000 rpm for
5 min to increase the slurry total solids (TS) content to 5–6%. Namely,
equal amounts of DW or NBW and corn straw were added to repeat the
above steps for 6 times, totally about 214 days for this pre-augmentation
operation. All the experiments were conducted in triplicate. The concen-
trated AD efﬂuent was used as inoculum for the high-solids AD process in
Section 2.4.
2.3. Microbial community analysis
In order to identify the potential players in the biodegradation of corn
straw during the augmentation process, the sludge samples were collected
at the last bioaugmentation cycle for high-throughput 16S rRNA gene se-
quencing. The microbial DNA was extracted using the E.Z.N.A.® soil
DNA Kit (Omega Bio-tek, Norcross, GA, US) according to the manufactur-
er’s protocols. The primers 338F (5′-ACTCCTACGGGAG GCAGCAG-3′)
and 806R (5′-GGACTACHVGGGTWTCTAAT-3′) were used to amplify the
V3–V4 region of bacterial 16S rRNA (GeneAmp 9700, ABI, USA). The ar-
chaeal 16S rDNA was ampliﬁed with the primer pair of 524F10extF (5′-
TGYCAGCCGCCGCGGTAA-3′) and Arch958RmodR (5′-YCCGGCGTTG
AVTCCAATT-3′). According to the standard protocol of Majorbio Bio-
Pharm Technology Co. Ltd. (Shanghai, China), the puriﬁed amplicons
were combined on an Illumina MiSeq platform (Illumina, San Diego,
USA) with equimolar and paired end sequencing (2 × 300 bp).
2.4. Biochemical methane potential (BMP) of corn straw via high-solids AD
High-solids AD of corn straw was performed in 100 mL closed Schott
Duran serum bottles. In these bottles, the added mass weight of inoculum,
i.e., the DW or NBW bioaugmented anaerobically digested sludge was 40
g, and the added mass weight of corn straw was estimated based on the
F/M (VS basis) ratio of 3. The initial TS contents in all the reactors were
14–15% (high-solids AD). The bottles only loaded with the inoculum
were prepared as blanks to eliminate the methane production amount
from high-solids AD of the same dose inoculum only (without corn
straw). Afterwards, all the treatment bottles were capped with rubber stop-
pers, ﬂushed with N2 gas for 5 min to create anaerobic condition, and
placed in a temperature-controlled incubator (35 ± 1 °C). The reactors
were manually shaken twice at ﬁxed time points every day. Biogas volume
was quantiﬁed by a 20 mL glass syringe connecting to the bottle, and biogas
components were analyzed by a GC-8A/TCD (Shimadzu, Japan). The sam-
ples from each reactor were collected to analyze the cellulose, hemicellu-
lose, and lignin contents, etc. All the sample analyses were conducted in
duplicate.
2.5. Analytical methods for other parameters
TS and VS were measured by following the Standard Methods (APHA,
2012). pH was determined with a semi-solid pH meter (Testo 206,
Germany). The contents of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin were quan-
tiﬁed according to the procedures described elsewhere (Wang et al.,
2020a). The activities of CMCase and xylanase were measured according
to Weiβ et al. (2010). LiP activity was determined as the oxidation rate of
veratryl alcohol by veratraldyde according to Pollegioni et al. (2015). The
heating value (labeled herein as E) of corn straw during direct combustion
was determined by a calorimeter (CA-4AJ, Shimadzu, Japan) after being
dried at 60 °C till constant weight.

ciency of the whole NBW-based high-solids AD system according to its sim-
pliﬁed operation model as follows: The disposal of corn straw was assumed

AD system, the input energy (Einput) for the digester was calculated as the
energy required according to Eq. (1) modiﬁed from He et al. (2017).

2.7. Statistical analysis
One-way analysis of variance analysis was performed for statistical val-
idation of the obtained results by using Origin 2019 software to estimate
the signiﬁcant difference among the treatments. A probability (p value)
<0.05 was termed as signiﬁcant. All data were calculated using Microsoft
Ofﬁce Excel 2020.
3. Results and discussion
3.1. Changes in performance of anaerobically digested sludge and its microorgan-
isms during bioaugmentation
3.1.1. Methane production
In order to enhance the functions of microbes that can produce methane
from AD of corn straw, NBW was added to augment the digested sludge for
6 cycles (214 days) with corn straw as the sole substrate in the AD process,
and the DW-added reactor was used as the control. Fig. 1 shows the cumu-
lative methane production during the augmentation process, which in-
creased along with the proceeding of the augmentation cycles. In the ﬁrst
augmentation cycle, no signiﬁcant difference (p > 0.6) was observed in
the methane yields from the DW, N2-NBW, and O2-NBW reactors. The
methane yields were gradually enhanced along with the augmentation cy-
cles; at the end of the 6th augmentation cycle, the methane yields were in-
creased by 20.0%, 29.7%, and 43.6% from the DW, N2-NBW and O2-NBW

3

reactors, respectively when compared to their 1st augmentation cycle. The
O2-NBW reactors obviously achieved the highest methane yield from AD of
corn straw, about 20.3% higher than that from the DW reactors. Nguyen
and Khanal (2018) claimed that microaerobic environment could enhance
diversity and activity of facultative heterotrophs resulting in improved hy-
drolysis of substrates. As for the two kinds of NBWs, O2-NBW showed better
enhancement effect on methane yield than N2-NBW, most probably due to
the microaerobic environment created by O2-NBW addition. In addition,
O2-NBs were observed to favor the generation of •OH radicals compared
to N2-NBs (Li et al., 2009). The oxygen-containing function groups can as-
sist the degradation of lignocellulosic biomass (Yang et al., 2020). These
previous works to some extent explained why the O2-NBW reactors
achieved higher methane production from AD of corn straw, most probably
attributable to the facilitated facultative anaerobes, thus contributing to the
enhanced hydrolysis stage in the AD process. The higher methane yield
from lignocellulosic biomass may also be partially associated with the en-
hanced enzymatic activities and the augmented microorganisms that de-
grade lignocellulosic biomass.
3.1.2. Activities of related enzymes
CMCase can break down the β-(1,4)-glycosidic linkages and release glu-
cose monomers (Karim et al., 2015), reﬂecting the degradability of cellu-
lose in corn straw. Seen from Figs. 2a and b, after 6 cycles’ augmentation,
the CMCase activity was increased by 7.2%, 2.2%, and 2.5% in the DW,
N2-NBW, and O2-NBW reactors, respectively. As for xylanase activity, the
enhancement effect was more obviously, about 12.8%, 41.5%, and 54.6%
increase in the DW, N2-NBW and O2-NBW reactors, respectively. Therefore,
NBW addition could also be developed as a new strategy for AD systems to
improve enzymatic activities. Among the test conditions, O2-NBW supple-
mentation might be the most efﬁcient, with the highest CMCase and
xylanase activities after the 6th bioaugmentation cycle, about 3.6% and
54.6% higher than those in the DW reactors, respectively. As Kholif et al.
(2017) pointed out, the increased CMCase and xylanases activities may
contribute to the improved methane production from AD of lignocellulose,
which to some extent explained why methane yield was detected to in-
crease in the DW or NBW bioaugmentation process. Seen from Fig. 2c,
LiP activity was increased by 0.7%, 46.5%, and 4.3% in the DW, N2-
NBW, and O2-NBW reactors after 214 days of augmentation, respectively.
Lignin generally acts as a physical barrier hindering the accessibility of cel-
lulose and hemicellulose to hydrolytic enzyme (Pang et al., 2021), leading
to a low hydrolysis efﬁciency of corn straw. LiP can speciﬁcally oxidize the
lignin polymers, thus enhancing its hydrolysis process which is the limiting
step for AD of lignocellulosic biomass (Sánchez, 2009). The NBW-
bioaugmented sludge could improve the hydrolysis of corn straw and
then enhance the biodegradation of lignocellulosic biomass. Therefore, re-
sults from this work are very promising and could be potentially used for
the development of an efﬁcient high-solids AD process to manage lignocel-
lulosic biomass for renewable energy production.
In the NBW reactors, the negatively charged surface of NBs may weaken
the hydrogen bond network in the liquid phase (Chaplin, 2007). The ad-
sorption of H+ ions on the surface of NBs, and the movement or absence
of protons in the liquid may trigger the modiﬁcation or destruction of the
hydrogen bond network (Chaplin, 2007). The weaken hydrogen bonds
can cause the reduction in liquid viscosity (Ma et al., 2018), resulting
in accelerated disintegration of lignocellulosic biomass and increased
accessibility to the fermentative bacteria, which may further improve
the hydrolysis efﬁciency of lignocellulosic biomass in the high-solids
AD. In addition, the longer proton spin-spin relaxation time reﬂects
the high mobility and diffusion of water molecules in NBW (Wang
et al., 2020b), contributing to its high mass transfer efﬁciency with im-
proved enzymatic activities (Alheshibri et al., 2016). The O2-NBW reac-
tors achieved the highest activities of hydrolytic enzymes in the AD of
corn straw, possibly attributable to the highest metabolic activities of
microbes owing to the improved electron transfer activity under the
test conditions (Wang et al., 2021). After NBW bioaugmentation, the
anaerobic microbes may keep their improved activities of hydrolytic en-
zymes and continue to exhibit high efﬁcacy of degrading lignocellulose
in the high-solids AD of corn straw. As known, variations of enzymatic
activities in biological processes are associated with the shift of micro-
bial communities. Therefore, the intrinsic mechanisms involved in the
enhanced enzymatic activities and methane production from AD of
corn straw by NBW-bioaugmented sludge deserve further elucidation
in view of the changes in microbial communities.
3.1.3. Changes in microbial community structure
Microbial community composition is a major driving factor for the deg-
radation of corn straw in AD, which is also an indicator of the activity of
NBW-bioaugmented sludge. In order to better understand the role of
NBW in the bioaugmentation process, microbial communities of the seed
anaerobically digested sludge and three sludge samples from the DW, N2-
NBW, and O2-NBW reactors after 214 days’ augmentation were analyzed
by high-throughput sequencing of 16S rRNA gene amplicons.

As shown in Fig. 3a, a number of microbial groups associated with the
biodegradation of corn straw were found, which were positively inﬂuenced
by NBW. The relative abundances (RAs) of phyla Acidobacteria,
Armatimonadetes, Atribacteria, Chloroﬂexi, Firmicutes, Spirochaetes, and
Synergistetes were increased, while the RAs of Bacteroidetes and
Proteobacteria were declined in the NBW bioaugmented reactors.
Atribacteria belongs to heterotrophic anaerobes that can ferment propio-
nate to produce acetic acid, thus resulting in enhanced methanogenesis
(Hoshino et al., 2017). Chloroﬂexi can utilize and degrade carbohydrates
at the initial stage of AD (hydrolysis and acidiﬁcation) (Ma et al., 2019),
which was more abundant in the NBW-bioaugmented reactors compared
to the DW reactors. Although Firmicutes were detected in all the sludge
samples, while the RAs of this phylum in the NBW reactors were higher
than the DW reactors (6.2%, 15.1%, and 8.9% in the DW, N2-NBW, and
O2-NBW reactors, respectively). However, without bioaugmentation,
Firmicutes reached only 3.6% in AD of lignocellulosic biomass with O2-
NBW supplementation (Wang et al., 2020c). Firmicutes are claimed to pro-
duce extracellular enzymes (e.g., CMCase and proteases) and can work well
under microaerobic condition to hydrolyze complex substrates (Fu et al.,
2016). This may offer a reasonable explanation for the higher enzymatic ac-
tivity (such as CMCase) in the NBW bioaugmentation reactors. In addition,
Firmicutes can also utilize organics to produce volatile fatty acids (VFAs)
and facilitate methane production. Spirochaetes are hydrolytic bacteria,
which can convert carbon sources to VFAs and then to acetic acid, H2 and
CO2 (Zhang et al., 2018). Synergistetes can well function in acetogenesis
and accelerate the conversion of VFAs to acetate (Lee et al., 2009). As

Methanobacterium was detected in the O2-NBW reactors, averagely reaching
7.1%, which belongs to hydrogen-consuming methanogens that can con-
sume CO2 and H2 to produce methane (Yuan et al., 2020). Under no bioaug-
mentation condition, Wang et al. (2020b) noticed only 1% increase of
Methanobacterium in AD of cellulose with NBW supplementation. Thus,
NBW bioaugmentation may signiﬁcantly enrich Methanobacterium se-
quences. As reported, Methanobacterium could be signiﬁcantly enhanced
under microaerobic conditions (Fu et al., 2016). These observations may
explain why the highest RA of Methanobacterium was detected in the O2-
NBW bioaugmented sludge, probably due to that O2-NBW may provide a
proper microaerobic condition (because of O2-NBs collapse to release
trace O2) that is beneﬁcial for the growth of Methanobacterium. Wang
et al. (2020c) veriﬁed that the microaerobic conditions provided by O2-
NBW exhibited positive effects on the methanogenesis stage of AD process.
In addition, the RAs of Methanosarcina in the DW, N2-NBW, and O2-NBW re-
actors were 11.7%, 1.0%, and 28.6%, respectively, higher than that in the
seed digested sludge. Methanosarcina has been reported to have direct inter-
species electron transfer (DIET) with Geobacter (Chen et al., 2014). The es-
tablishment of DIET between anaerobic fermentation bacteria and
methanogens can enhance AD of organic matters (Lü et al., 2016).
Methanosaeta can also directly accept electrons via DIET from Geobacter
and produce methane from CO2 reduction (Rotaru et al., 2014). A lower
RA of Methanosarcina was detected in the N2-NBW reactors, attributable
to the much greater proportion of Methanosaeta. The sum of RAs of
Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina were 78.6% and 66.7% in the N2-NBW
and O2-NBW reactors, about 23.9% and 5.1% higher than those in the
DW reactors, respectively. Therefore, the increase in the sum of RAs of
Methanosaeta and Methanosarcina in the NBW reactors may suggest the
DIET occurrence due to NBW supplementation. This phenomenon agrees
with the stimulation effect on microbial community by NBW supplementa-
tion (Wang et al., 2020c). These enhancements of microorganisms in the
NBW reactors may imply the accelerated hydrolysis and methanogenesis
stages of AD of corn straw when compared with the seed digested sludge.
In summary, the O2-NBW reactors achieved the highest methane pro-
duction (Fig. 1), most probably attributable to the microaerobic condition
created by O2-NBW. The high stability of O2-NBs can continue to be the po-
tent O2 suppliers in the liquid (Ebina et al., 2013), which could provide O2
into medium slowly and last for a longer time when compared with the or-
dinary O2 aeration. In addition, the hydrophilicity and the high mobility of
NBs can enhance the accessibility of microorganisms to corn straw in AD
process, which could provide abundant nutrient and carbon sources for
the growth of microorganisms, further enriching microbial communities.
The addition of O2-NBW may realize a delicate balance which not only fa-
cilitates the metabolism of facultative bacteria but also improves the enzy-
matic activities of microorganisms (Wang et al., 2021). NBW can generate
numerous reactive oxygen species (ROS), including hydroxyl radicals
(•OH), superoxide anion radicals (O2
−), and singlet oxygen (1O2) during
the process of NBs collapse. Shi et al. (2021) found the oxygen-containing
function groups could facilitate the occurrence of DIET in AD process.
Therefore, free radicals produced from NBs collapse may enhance the ligno-
cellulosic biomass degradation. In the previous works, NBs in NBW were
claimed to almost disappear and no large bubbles were observed after stor-
age at room temperature for one month (Wang et al., 2020c; Yang et al.,
2019; Wang et al., 2019). Therefore, it’s hypothesized that the NBs collapse
occurs and disappears in the liquid. However, the stable existence time of
NBs still remains a big challenge. Currently the NBW studies are at the pre-
liminary stage, and the disappearance mechanism of NBs in liquid needs to
be further explored by using the innovative technologies. Still, some direct
evidence is demanding for the above viewpoints in the followed-up works.
3.2. Use of bioaugmented sludge for BMP tests on high-solids AD of corn straw
3.2.1. Degradation of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin
During the high-solids AD of corn straw, the three major organic compo-
nents were found to decrease obviously, with the largest reduction being
detected in hemicellulose (Fig. 4). As seen, the contents of cellulose, hemi-
cellulose, and lignin in the NBW reactors were averagely reduced to
10.9–13.6%, 7.5–8.8%, and 6.3–6.4% (p < 0.05), respectively in compari-
son to 16.2%, 8.5%, and 7.3% in the DW reactors. These results suggest
that the NBW-bioaugmented sludge exhibited higher degradation capabili-
ties for lignin and cellulose. In addition, the O2-NBW bioaugmented sludge
seemed to have the highest lignocellulosic biomass degradation capability
than the N2-NBW and DW counterparts, with cellulose, hemicellulose,
and lignin reduced by about 50.4%, 60.0%, and 31.7%, respectively (p <
0.05). This observation suggests that the degradation capability of lignocel-
lulose in corn straw follows a descending order of hemicellulose > cellulose
> lignin in the high-solids AD. Seen from Section 3.1.3, a signiﬁcant enrich-
ment of hydrolytic/acidogenic bacteria and methanogenic archaea was no-
ticed in the O2-NBW bioaugmented sludge compared to the N2-NBW
reactors. Therefore, the O2-NBW bioaugmented sludge also possessed the
highest total lignocellulose (cellulose+hemicellulose+lignin) degradation
potential, about 51% reduction in lignocellulose content in corn straw,
followed by the N2-NBW (44%) and DW (36%) bioaugmented sludge, re-
spectively. NBW-based high-solids AD technology was found to be able to
efﬁciently hydrolyze cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin, resulting in high
efﬁciency methane production and energy recovery from corn straw.

almost no biogas production from the blank reactors (only the inoculum,
or the bioaugmented sludge with DW, N2-NBW or O2-NBW addition). Dur-
ing the ﬁrst eight days, little methane production was detected from all the

reactors possess higher hydrolysis capacity of lignocellulosic biomass due
to the enriched hydrolytic bacteria. Therefore, these reactors may produce
more VFAs, leading to a lower local pH microenvironment, which may in-
hibit the rapid growth of methanogens. Further in-depth studies are still
necessary on the activity of methanogens during this early stage of high-
solids AD, and the possible solutions or strategies for this delayed methane
production as well. More speciﬁcally, during days 0–28, the lowest meth-

This observation may be more associated with the micro‑oxygen environ-
ment favoring the enrichment of facultative bacteria to degrade corn
straw (Fu et al., 2016), which might result in the lowest pH microenviron-
ment (data not shown). When the small molecular intermediates were grad-
ually consumed, the local pH microenvironment would return to neutral
along with the operation, resulting in higher methane production during
the later stage.
As seen, during the 70 days’ BMP tests, the cumulative methane yields
from corn straw in the N2-NBW and O2-NBW reactors reached 144.2 ±
3.2 (p = 0.048 < 0.05) and 179.2 ± 5.2 (p = 0.010 < 0.05) NmL/g-VS, in-
creasing by 18.1% and 46.8% when compared to those from the DW reac-
tors (averagely 122.1 ± 6.3 NmL/g-VS). Compared with the result from He
et al. (2022) who achieved 12–25% increase in methane yields from AD of
corn straw with H2-NBW addition, the enhancement effect on methane pro-
duction from corn straw after NBW bioaugmentation is more prominent. In a
previous study, the theoretical methane production of corn straw was 223.3
mL/g-VS according to the elemental composition (C, H, N and O) of corn
straw (Wang et al., 2020a). The highest biodegradability of corn straw was
achieved in the O2-NBW pre-augmented sludge reactors, about 80%,
followed by N2-NBW (65%), and DW (55%). This enhancement effect on
methane production was mainly attributable to the enriched microbial com-
munities and enhanced enzymatic activities in this study. Up to today, the O2-
NBW-based high-solids AD system achieved the highest methane production
from corn straw among all the test NBW-based AD systems.
3.2.3. Energy balance analysis
Although the NBW-bioaugmented sludge reactors achieved some in-
crease in methane production during the 70 days’ high-solids AD of corn
straw, this increment of energy (methane) may be not enough to support
the energy consumption by maintaining the operation of AD reactors. In
this study, the energy balance was analyzed based on the BMP tests on
high-solids AD of corn straw according to Eqs. (1)–(4) (Table 1). The
heating value (E) of corn straw was determined as 15,160 ± 25 MJ/t-VScorn
straw. In fact, a positive net energy gain was achieved in all the reactors. It is
worth noting that the O2-NBW bioaugmented sludge reactors achieved the
highest net energy gain (ΔE = 5138.0 MJ/t-VScorn straw) and energy recov-
ery (η = 33.9%) through methane production from high-solids AD of corn
straw, followed by N2-NBW (ΔE = 4010.3 MJ/t-VScorn straw, 26.5%) and
DW (ΔE = 3298.3 MJ/t-VScorn straw, 21.8%) bioaugmented sludge reactors,
respectively. These results clearly highlight the much greater net energy
gain from the high-solids AD of corn straw when the O2-NBW
bioaugmented sludge was applied, increasing by 55.8% in net energy
gain and 55.5% in energy recovery respectively when compared to the con-
trol (DW bioaugmented sludge reactors). This is mainly attributable to the
much higher methane production (about 47% increase) from the O2-NBW
bioaugmented sludge reactors (Table 1 and Fig. 5).
3.3. Implications of NBW-based high-solids AD systems
Improper handling (like incineration) or disposal of corn straw would
cause negative effects on human health and the environment, which gener-
ally occurs in most developing countries. NBW-based high-solids AD can
not only achieve sustainable management of lignocellulosic biomass but
also obtain high net energy gain from lignocellulosic biomass. NBW tech-
nology has been frequently trialed on AD of organic solid wastes due to
its unique characteristics and properties including nontoxicity and low en-
ergy consumption that could avoid secondary pollution and extra energy
consumption, targeting the sustainable development goals. The new con-
cept proposed in this study, including NBW bioaugmentation of anaerobi-
cally digested sludge and subsequent high-solids AD of lignocellulosic
biomass, can avoid the increase in reactor volume and the generation of liq-
uid digestate (wastewater), greatly improving the volumetric methane pro-
ductivity and thus lowering the investment and operation costs. This study
ﬁrst conﬁrmed that NBW bioaugmented AD sludge could achieve enhanced
methane yield and net energy gain from high-solids AD of corn straw,
clearly demonstrating the economic feasibility of the NBW-based high-
solids AD system for organic solid wastes. The apparent enhancement
roles of enzymatic activities and microbial communities are interesting
from both scientiﬁc and practical viewpoints, which may serve as potential
indicators for a well and stably operated high-solids AD reactor.
4. Conclusions
NBW bioaugmentation can obviously enhance the enzymatic activities
(2–55%) and microbial communities (7–9%) in anaerobically digested
sludge, especially lignocellulolytic microorganisms. Cellulose, hemicellu-
lose, and lignin reductions can also be enhanced in the NBW-based high-
solids AD systems. Results from this work can help better understand the
fundamentals involved. In this study, it was ﬁrst conﬁrmed that the NBW-
based high-solids AD technology could increase net energy gain by 56%
from corn straw when compared to the control. NBW-based high-solids

Corrigendum
Corrigendum to “Use of nanobubble water bioaugmented anaerobically 
digested sludge for high-efficacy energy production from high-solids 
anaerobic digestion of corn straw” [Sci. Total Environ. 863 (2023) 160825]
Xuezhi Wang a,c, Zhongfang Lei b,*, Zhenya Zhang b, Kazuya Shimizu b,d, Duu-Jong Lee e,  
Samir Kumar Khanal f

This Corrigendum relates to the above article.
In this article, the authors used wording that overstated the impli­
cations of the experimental results with respect to sustainability and 
economic feasibility. The study reported enhanced methane production 
and a positive process-level net energy balance under the laboratory 
conditions tested.
However, the study did not include a lifecycle assessment, techno- 
economic analysis, pilot-scale validation, or full environmental sus­
tainability assessment. The authors therefore wish to clarify that the 
results should be interpreted as evidence of process-level energy per­
formance, rather than as a demonstration of environmental sustain­
ability or economic feasibility.
The original version of Section 3.3 on page 7 is as below:
NBW-based high-solids AD can not only achieve sustainable man­
agement of lignocellulosic biomass but also obtain high net energy gain 
from lignocellulosic biomass. This study first confirmed that NBW bio­
augmented AD sludge could achieve enhanced methane yield and net 
energy gain from high-solids AD of corn straw, clearly demonstrating the 
economic feasibility of the NBW-based high-solids AD system for organic 
solid wastes.
The updated version should be as below:
The present study shows that nanobubble water bioaugmented 
anaerobically digested sludge can enhance methane production from 
corn straw and generate a positive process-level net energy balance 
under the tested laboratory conditions. These findings indicate the po­
tential of NBW-assisted high-solids anaerobic digestion for lignocellu­
losic biomass valorization and renewable energy recovery. However, the 
energy-balance calculation presented here should be interpreted as 
preliminary and process-specific and should not be taken as evidence of 
full environmental sustainability or economic feasibility. Further life­
cycle assessment, techno-economic analysis, and pilot- or full-scale 
validation are required before conclusions can be drawn on the 
broader sustainability, economic viability, and practical implementa­
tion of this approach.
